docs.text: Turn loop and phases Main objects GameState : NetworkedBehaviour is the match controller, one per match. It holds the players, islands, phase objects, Log , Chat , SnapshotStore , AIPlay , LobbySettings and a match-wide Unity.Mathematics.Random random . Island : NetworkedBehaviour belongs to one player: owner ( NetworkedVar<Player> , 0x90 ), grid ( IslandGrid , 0x98 ), statistics ( Statistics , 0xA0 : resources and learnt technologies). Player : NetworkedBehaviour : name, colour, skins / civilization, AI state, isDefeated , isAwaited , ping, start-game slot. Useful GameState fields: players 0xE8 , playerIds 0xF8 , lobbySettings 0xD0 , phaseOrder 0x170 , startPhase 0x178 , harvestPhase 0x180 , disastersPhase 0x188 , buildPhase 0x190 , combatPhase 0x198 , winPhase 0x1A0 , turnCounter ( NetworkedVar<int> ) 0x1B8 , TurnPhase 0x1C0 , IsTraining 0x1C8 . GameState has Action fields that are good hook points for mods: onIslandSpawned , onStartGame , onEnterPhase , onSyncPhase , onEndGame , onExit(string) , onReset , onRejoin , onDisasterLog(Player, StructuredText) . Phase order GameState.Awake ( 0x5F26A0 ) sets phaseOrder = [ HarvestPhase, DisastersPhase, BuildPhase, CombatPhase, WinPhase ] StartPhase ("Settle") is not in the loop: it runs once at the start of the match. Awake also seeds random , shuffles the player colours into teams and wraps the lobby settings in a NetworkedVar . Phase Time limit (timer FAST) Notes Start ("Settle") 60 s once per match Harvest 40 s (+5 s sync) Harvest and dice Disasters none ends when every client has played the animations, Disasters Build 70 s Build phase Combat 35 s planning time; the fight is simulated and animated afterwards, Combat Win none Win conditions Timer speed (lobby option TimerSpeed ): FAST ×1, SLOW ×1.5, UNLIMITED = no limit ( TurnPhase.get_TimeLimit 0xFE0460 ). Games with fewer than two human players are forced to UNLIMITED ( GameState.StartGame ). The values are fields of the phase components in the scene ( timeLimit , timeLimitSync ), not code. Phase states Each phase is a TurnPhase<TData, TIslandState> with a PhaseState : ACTIVE = 0 , SYNC = 1 , INACTIVE = 2 . For every island the phase holds one PhaseData object (for example BuildData ); per-player state is in islandStates (keyed by client id). GameState.UpdateTurnPhase ( 0x5F6E20 ) runs every frame: ACTIVE : when TurnPhase.IsReady() is true, call TurnPhase.Sync() . SYNC : when TurnPhase.IsSynced() is true, go to the next phase in phaseOrder whose ShouldSkip() is false. Wrapping from the last phase back to the first increments turnCounter . ChangeTurnPhase ( 0x5F2C20 ) calls old.Exit() then new.Enter(false) and flashes the taskbar if the window is not focused (not for a defeated player). The turn counter goes up when the Win phase wraps back to the Harvest phase. Ready TurnPhase.IsReady ( 0xFDD8B0 ): For every island: ready = IsReady(island) , and Player.IsAwaited = !ready (the "waiting for player" marker). False while the phase banner is still showing ( TimeSinceEnter < BannerDuration , 2 s). Otherwise true when all islands are ready , or when the timer ran out ( TimeRemaining < 0 ). An island is ready when its phase data has nothing to do, or the player pressed Ready ( PhaseData.Skip() → SkipRPC , flag HasSkipped ). Sync TurnPhase.Sync ( 0xFDEB40 ): Store syncTime ; the server sends SyncRPC(syncTime) to all clients. Server: for every island owned by an AI , call AIPlay.PlayPhase(phaseData, aiState) . The AI makes its moves when the phase ends, not during it. State = SYNC , fire GameState.onSyncPhase . Server: ApplyChanges(done) . Each phase overrides it to apply the planned actions of all players. After every phase's ApplyChanges , TurnPhase.Recompute recomputes every island (storage capacity, defeat). Entering a phase TurnPhase.Enter ( 0xFDCD00 ) runs on every machine. The server tells all clients to enter ( EnterRPC with the start time), every island's PhaseData.Enter runs (it also sets the Preview flag, see Build phase ), and on clients the phase's interface is enabled. It also sets the time of day: each phase has a timeOfDay field (all phases 0.125 = morning) that is written into the DayNightCycle target, see Rendering . Clock ITurnPhase.Time ( 0x56D8D0 ) is the clock all phases use. It returns Cheats.NetworkTime() : the network time multiplied by the developer speed factor. Start phase ("Settle") StartData.Reset ( 0x572C40 ) fills the island's BuildingsToPlace list: Castle, Cottage ×3, Farm, Dock . StartData.PlaceBuilding ( 0x5728C0 ) places one of them if the normal tile rules pass ( IslandGrid.CanPlaceBuilding ) and the type is still in the list; each listed type can be placed exactly as often as it appears. There is no check for buildings that already exist on the island: an island loaded from an island code that already has a Castle still gets the start Castle, so the player has two. At the end ( StartPhase.ApplyChanges 0x573370 ), for every island: Placed buildings are added (if they still fit). Every type still in BuildingsToPlace is placed automatically at IslandGrid.PlaceableBuilding(type) ( 0x6179E0 ). This happens whether the timer ran out or everybody pressed Ready. The island is recomputed and gets the start resources: 3 food, 3 wood, 2 stone, 4 hammers, 8 culture . PlaceableBuilding walks the island in a spiral from the centre outwards (the same spiral the AI uses), tries the 4 orientations without mirroring, and takes the first spot where CanPlaceBuilding passes and the building does not raise disease risk ( Disease.DoesRiskMoreDisease ). So auto-placed buildings end up as close to the island centre as allowed. (The AI places its farms far from the centre on purpose, see AI .) World layout GameState.SpawnIslands ( 0x5F3F70 ) runs on the server at game start with the match random generator, so the layout is the same for everybody. Island positions (one per player): g = island grid size (49 × 49 by default), halfDiag = √((g.x/2)² + (g.y/2)²) ≈ 34.6, step = halfDiag × 0.001. Starting at radius r = step , take a random point in an ellipse with radii (r × 16/9, r), turned 45°. Reject it if it overlaps an island already placed (|dx| ≤ g.x and |dy| ≤ g.y); otherwise r grows by step and it tries again. Islands are packed tightly, in a 16:9 oval turned 45°; more players make it wider. The points are sorted by angle around the origin and given to the players in list order, so neighbours in the player list are neighbours around the circle. Island shapes (fairness): 256 islands are generated and sorted by score (natural resources + build space + cliffs). Only the middle N (N = number of players) are kept and shuffled, so every player gets an island of about median quality. Generation itself: Island generation . A layout mod can postfix SpawnIslands to move islands or replace grids, but it must run on the host so every client gets the same world. Snapshots and rejoin TurnPhase.TakeSnapshot stores (Island, IslandGrid.SyncData, Statistics.SyncData) for every island when a phase is entered; SnapshotStore keeps them under (player, turn, phase) . GameState.Restore() , RestoreTurnPhase and Rejoin(Player) let a player who reconnects rebuild the state ( PhaseData.RejoinClientRPC ). Training GameState.IsTraining is the tutorial game (strings training.information.* ).

docs.text: GameState : NetworkedBehaviour is the match controller, one per match. It holds the players, islands, phase objects, Log , Chat , SnapshotStore , AIPlay , LobbySettings and a match-wide Unity.Mathematics.Random random . Island : NetworkedBehaviour belongs to one player: owner ( NetworkedVar<Player> , 0x90 ), grid ( IslandGrid , 0x98 ), statistics ( Statistics , 0xA0 : resources and learnt technologies). Player : NetworkedBehaviour : name, colour, skins / civilization, AI state, isDefeated , isAwaited , ping, start-game slot. Useful GameState fields: players 0xE8 , playerIds 0xF8 , lobbySettings 0xD0 , phaseOrder 0x170 , startPhase 0x178 , harvestPhase 0x180 , disastersPhase 0x188 , buildPhase 0x190 , combatPhase 0x198 , winPhase 0x1A0 , turnCounter ( NetworkedVar<int> ) 0x1B8 , TurnPhase 0x1C0 , IsTraining 0x1C8 . GameState has Action fields that are good hook points for mods: onIslandSpawned , onStartGame , onEnterPhase , onSyncPhase , onEndGame , onExit(string) , onReset , onRejoin , onDisasterLog(Player, StructuredText) .

docs.text: Game UI The interface is Unity uGUI with TextMeshPro. The facts below were collected from the game version 1.0.4. Canvases Canvas Notes [Graphy] Overlay of the performance display, sorting order 30000. Canvas Over Dice , Canvas Background , Canvas Screen Space - Camera, sorting 0, reference resolution 1920x1080 (scale 1). The HUD is under Canvas . Mod windows are parented to the HUD canvas (found through components such as BuildInterface , ChatInterface , LogInterface ). Buttons Game buttons are components of the game, not plain Unity colours: DiceKingdoms.Interface.BaseButton holds the Unity Button ( unityButton ), the state, per-state cursor sprites, the Interactable property and the onClick event. BaseButton.Update maps the texture of the shown sprite to a state, so a button must always keep one of its known sprites. Subclasses: ButtonIcon (an icon, used by the top-right bar: Top > Icon ) and ButtonLabel (a text button: Top > Label ). Art: Button-1-{Ready,Hovered,Pressed,Disabled} (384x384, 9-slice border 32, pixels per unit 200, type Sliced, 32x32 units in the HUD). Button-2-* is the second style, used for the selected look. The Unity Button uses a sprite swap, plus a Shadow component. A sliced button needs a size of about twice its border. At exactly 32 units the centre slice is empty and rounding leaves hairlines. Label: TextMeshProUGUI , font Main-Font-Normal , size 20 with auto size, colour RGBA(0.969, 0.940, 0.893), material Main-Font-Normal-Shadow , centred. Windows and frames Window background: an Image with sprite Background-3 (2048x2048, Simple, white with alpha about 0.95; Background-4 is used less) and a child Ornament-N (Sliced, white). Ornament borders: 1 = 16, 2 = 142, 3 = 32 (most used), 4 = 32, 5 = 150. Fonts: TMP assets Main-Font-Normal (almost every text) and Main-Font-Big ; materials Main-Font-Normal-Shadow , Main-Font-Big-Shadow , Main-Font-Normal-Flat . Icons: hammer (512x512), settings, back-to-menu, question-mark, and building-icon-<type>-ancient-<colour> (256x280). Top-right bar Canvas > Meta > Buttons is a HorizontalLayoutGroup with a ContentSizeFitter (anchors top right, 140x32), so its children flow automatically. The children are 32x32: Scoreboard, Rules (the "?" icon, opens the long rules screen), Settings, Back To Menu. Each has Top > Icon (24x24). In the main menu the same style is under Top Right/Top Right Buttons . The Rules button has one persistent click listener, which must be removed when it is cloned. Scenes The Rules screen, Settings screen, About, Store and Scoreboard are separate screens that exist in the hierarchy but may be inactive. Cloning a template from an inactive screen works, but the screen must have been loaded. Settings rows and the lobby settings box The Settings window ( SettingSetsInterface ) has four tabs ( Video , Audio , Input , Game ), each a SettingSetInterface with a Vertical Scroll ( ScrollRect ) whose Viewport is a RectMask2D and whose Content is a VerticalLayoutGroup + ContentSizeFitter . The settings box of the match-start screen (the "Lobby" tab) is built the same way, 430x424 units. SettingSetInterface.GenerateElements fills Content with an entry per setting; rows are made from prefabs the set references ( settingEntryInterfacePrefab , settingInterfacePrefabs ). Entry: Setting Entry is a HorizontalLayoutGroup + SettingEntryInterface with a Label (125 wide in the lobby box) and a Content holder ( contentHolder ). In the lobby box the holder is 305 wide and a VerticalLayoutGroup ; in the other tabs it is 500 wide and has no layout group. Its width is 0 until the layout has run, so a row that needs the width has to measure it again later. Controls put into a holder with a layout group are stretched or stacked by it. Controls: SettingInterfaceBool (a checkbox, Toggle ), SettingInterfaceFloat (the slider of the Frame Rate Limit setting), SettingInterfaceDropdown<T> / SettingInterfaceEnum* , SettingInterfaceInputPath , SettingInterfaceLobbyCode . Each is bound to a Setting<T> of a SettingSet ; a clone has no setting, so the binding component is destroyed before the clone wakes up ( SettingInterfaceFloat.Awake adds a slider listener that writes setting.Value and would throw on every drag otherwise). Slider row: Label (the value text, 34 wide) + Slider > Background (4 high), Fill Area > Fill , Handle Slide Area > Handle (20 wide, the height of the slider). The handle is round only when the slider's rectangle is as tall as the handle is wide (20), and it sticks out about 5-10 units past both ends of the track, so the track must stay clear of any clipping edge. Scroll view of the lobby box: the Viewport mask is as big as the whole frame (430x424), so a row scrolled to the edge is drawn over the frame's yellow border (the game's own rows never reach it); the clip can be pulled in with RectMask2D.padding (2 units is the border's width). The Scroll Bar is 6x418 and spans the frame; its Handle has a Shadow , which at the bottom of the track hangs out of the frame. The lobby box shows only the game's own rows in the unmodded game (they fit, so it does not scroll); once a mod adds rows, the scrollbar, the clip and the row widths all matter. Canvas size and aspect ratio The game's canvases use CanvasScaler in ScaleWithScreenSize mode with a 1920x1080 reference. The scene data (not the code) decides the match mode, and it differs between the two scenes (confirmed in game by switching the window between aspect ratios and logging the canvas sizes): In a match , all three canvases ( Canvas , Canvas Over Dice , Canvas Background ) match width : always 1920 units wide, height = 1920 / ratio. In the main menu , the Canvas matches height : always 1080 units tall, width = 1080 x ratio. Ratio Match canvases Main menu canvas 16:9 1920x1080 1920x1080 16:10 1920x1200 1728x1080 4:3 1920x1440 1440x1080 5:4 1920x1536 1350x1080 21:9 1920x823 2520x1080 32:9 1920x540 3840x1080 So on a wide screen the match HUD gets shorter (a 21:9 screen has only 823 units of height for the HUD), and on a 4:3 or 5:4 screen it gets taller. Everything that is sized in units (the lobby box, setting rows, windows) scales with the screen. Anything placed by its top-left corner must be kept inside the canvas when the size changes. Canvas.scaleFactor (screen pixels per unit) is what a mouse delta has to be divided by when dragging.

docs.text: Win conditions There are only two ways to win: military (everybody else is out) and wonder victory (lobby option, on by default). WinState { winnerRef, reason (MILITARY 0 / WONDER 1), turn } . Defeat TurnPhase.RecomputeIsDefeated ( 0xFDE040 ): Player.IsDefeated = !island.grid.buildings.Any(b => b.type is BuildingTypeCastle) A player is out when no Castle is left : destroyed in combat, by a disaster (a tsunami touching it), or burnt by the player (see Build phase ). It is recomputed for every island after every phase's ApplyChanges , so it is not permanent : if a Castle exists again (for example from an island code), the player is back in. Losing a Castle IslandGrid.RemoveBuilding ( 0x619360 ) runs for every removed building (burn, combat, disasters). It clears the tiles and leaves remains (walls do not leave remains). If the building is a Castle: IslandGrid.BurnAllBuildings ( 0x613A80 ) removes every building that is not a Castle , in order of distance from the Castle with a growing delay (the spreading fire). Statistics.SetCapacity(ZERO) : all storage capacity becomes 0, which also empties everything stored , hammers included. The capacity comes back at the end of the phase (from the remaining buildings), but the stored amounts stay at 0. Several Castles (possible with an island code ): other Castles are not burnt, and the player is not defeated while any Castle is left (confirmed in game: burning one of three Castles burnt everything else, the other two stayed and the game went on). Because the hammers are gone, only one Castle can be burnt per build phase. Free-for-all WinPhase.CheckWin ( 0x57AB10 ): a game with only one island never ends by itself. Otherwise it calls CheckWinTeam when the lobby option Teams is on, else CheckWinFFA ( 0x579EA0 ): alive = islands whose owner is not defeated. alive == 0 → draw (it happens when the last players lose their last Castle in the same combat phase). alive == 1 → that player wins, reason military . Otherwise, with wonder victory on: sort by WonderCount . If the top player has more Wonders than the second, they win with reason wonder , at turn = WonderBuildTurn(top, second + 1) + 1 ( WONDER_TURN_DELAY = 1 ): the turn after the leader first had more Wonders than anyone else, so the others get one turn to answer (destroy it or build their own). A tie: nobody wins. So in free-for-all the match ends only when one player is left : a human losing does not end a match that still has two or more AIs. Gold for a victory needs at least 5 turns (see Lobby and Steam ). WinNow ( 0x57B340 ) applies a win once its turn has come; ShouldSkip ( 0x57B2D0 ) skips the Win phase when no win is due. WinRPC broadcasts it. Teams CheckWinTeam ( 0x57A410 ): Collect the teams of all players that are not defeated. None → draw. Exactly one → that team wins (military); the stored winner is the first such player in the player list. Two or more teams → only a wonder win: teams are compared by MaxWonderCount , the most Wonders any single player of the team has (teammates' Wonders are not added together). The winner turn is MinWonderBuildTurn(top team, second team's count + 1) + 1 . End screen WinInterface.PlayAnimation ( 0x5EEA70 ): The camera flies to the winner's island (on a draw: your own island). Title: a draw text, or one text with the winner: the team in team mode, the player name in free-for-all. The losing player sees the same "Victory!" title with the winner's name. Icon: draw → icon 7, military → the sword (icon 6), wonder → the winner's Wonder icon in their player colour. Continue closes the screen and leaves you as a spectator: free camera, your scoreboard row shows a skull, empty resources, inactive build menu. As a defeated player every island's actions are shown instantly ( Preview ). The "imminent victory" warning (a Wonder win coming next turn) shows for 6 s and fades out in 1 s ( ImminentVictoryWarning ).
docs.title: Win Conditions

docs.text: There are only two ways to win: military (everybody else is out) and wonder victory (lobby option, on by default). WinState { winnerRef, reason (MILITARY 0 / WONDER 1), turn } .
docs.title: Win conditions

docs.text: TurnPhase.RecomputeIsDefeated ( 0xFDE040 ): Player.IsDefeated = !island.grid.buildings.Any(b => b.type is BuildingTypeCastle) A player is out when no Castle is left : destroyed in combat, by a disaster (a tsunami touching it), or burnt by the player (see Build phase ). It is recomputed for every island after every phase's ApplyChanges , so it is not permanent : if a Castle exists again (for example from an island code), the player is back in.
docs.title: Defeat

docs.text: IslandGrid.RemoveBuilding ( 0x619360 ) runs for every removed building (burn, combat, disasters). It clears the tiles and leaves remains (walls do not leave remains). If the building is a Castle: IslandGrid.BurnAllBuildings ( 0x613A80 ) removes every building that is not a Castle , in order of distance from the Castle with a growing delay (the spreading fire). Statistics.SetCapacity(ZERO) : all storage capacity becomes 0, which also empties everything stored , hammers included. The capacity comes back at the end of the phase (from the remaining buildings), but the stored amounts stay at 0. Several Castles (possible with an island code ): other Castles are not burnt, and the player is not defeated while any Castle is left (confirmed in game: burning one of three Castles burnt everything else, the other two stayed and the game went on). Because the hammers are gone, only one Castle can be burnt per build phase.
docs.title: Losing a Castle

docs.text: WinPhase.CheckWin ( 0x57AB10 ): a game with only one island never ends by itself. Otherwise it calls CheckWinTeam when the lobby option Teams is on, else CheckWinFFA ( 0x579EA0 ): alive = islands whose owner is not defeated. alive == 0 → draw (it happens when the last players lose their last Castle in the same combat phase). alive == 1 → that player wins, reason military . Otherwise, with wonder victory on: sort by WonderCount . If the top player has more Wonders than the second, they win with reason wonder , at turn = WonderBuildTurn(top, second + 1) + 1 ( WONDER_TURN_DELAY = 1 ): the turn after the leader first had more Wonders than anyone else, so the others get one turn to answer (destroy it or build their own). A tie: nobody wins. So in free-for-all the match ends only when one player is left : a human losing does not end a match that still has two or more AIs. Gold for a victory needs at least 5 turns (see Lobby and Steam ). WinNow ( 0x57B340 ) applies a win once its turn has come; ShouldSkip ( 0x57B2D0 ) skips the Win phase when no win is due. WinRPC broadcasts it.
docs.title: Free-for-all

docs.text: CheckWinTeam ( 0x57A410 ): Collect the teams of all players that are not defeated. None → draw. Exactly one → that team wins (military); the stored winner is the first such player in the player list. Two or more teams → only a wonder win: teams are compared by MaxWonderCount , the most Wonders any single player of the team has (teammates' Wonders are not added together). The winner turn is MinWonderBuildTurn(top team, second team's count + 1) + 1 .
docs.title: Teams

docs.text: WinInterface.PlayAnimation ( 0x5EEA70 ): The camera flies to the winner's island (on a draw: your own island). Title: a draw text, or one text with the winner: the team in team mode, the player name in free-for-all. The losing player sees the same "Victory!" title with the winner's name. Icon: draw → icon 7, military → the sword (icon 6), wonder → the winner's Wonder icon in their player colour. Continue closes the screen and leaves you as a spectator: free camera, your scoreboard row shows a skull, empty resources, inactive build menu. As a defeated player every island's actions are shown instantly ( Preview ). The "imminent victory" warning (a Wonder win coming next turn) shows for 6 s and fades out in 1 s ( ImminentVictoryWarning ).

docs.text: Island Generation The island generation system turns a seed and a set of tuning parameters into a playable island. It runs in two stages: first the tile stage - every grid cell gets a ground type and possibly a nature object; then the mesh stage - the tile layer is turned into a PolygonMesh with a HeightMap . Both stages are Burst‑compiled IJob s launched from static methods of IslandGeneration . IslandGeneration IslandGeneration is the central class responsible for the entire island generation pipeline. The bodies of nested types ( Parameters , NoiseLayers , GenerateJob , etc.) are expanded in the following sections. namespace DiceKingdoms.Game ; public static class IslandGeneration { public static float EPSILON ; public static float WATER_MAX_DEPTH ; public sealed class ConnectedComponents < T > : Il2CppSystem . ValueType { /* section "References" */ } [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Explicit)] public struct NoiseLayers { /* section "NoiseLayers" */ } public sealed class GenerateOutput : Il2CppSystem . ValueType { /* section "GenerateOutput" */ } public sealed class GenerateJob : Il2CppSystem . ValueType { /* section "GenerateJob" */ } public sealed class HeightMap : Il2CppSystem . ValueType { /* section "HeightMap" */ } public struct Bounds { /* section "Bounds" */ } public sealed class MeshOutput : Il2CppSystem . ValueType { /* section "MeshOutput" */ } public sealed class MeshJob : Il2CppSystem . ValueType { /* section "MeshJob" */ } public static GenerateOutput Generate ( ref Parameters parameters , ref IEnumerable < InnerCliff . Key > innerCliffKeys , ref int2 size , ref uint seed ); public static MeshOutput BuildMesh ( IslandGrid . Layer < GroundTile > layer , Biome biome , int heightMapSubdivide , PolygonMesh lavaTileMesh , PolygonMesh pierTileMesh ); public static PolygonMesh BuildAltitudeMesh ( ref Parameters parameters , float2 center , int2 size , ref Unity . Mathematics . Random random ); public static PolygonMesh BuildHeightMapMesh ( IslandGrid . Layer < GroundTile > layer , Biome biome , int heightMapSubdivide , PolygonMesh lavaTileMesh , PolygonMesh pierTileMesh ); public static void HeightMapFromMesh ( ref PolygonMesh mesh , ref HeightMap heightMap ); public static void MaxFilter ( ref HeightMap heightMap , ref float radius ); private static ConnectedComponents < T > ComputeConnectedComponents < T , P > ( UnsafeLayer < T > layer , P predicate , Allocator allocator ) where T : unmanaged ; } Generation is split into two sequential stages. The first stage - tiles. The entry point is Generate(ref parameters, ref innerCliffKeys, ref size, ref seed) . First, NoiseLayers.Generate(...) is called: it fixes random offsets for the altitude and moisture noise and produces NoiseLayers - an immutable struct from which Altitude(position) and Moisture(position) can later be sampled. Then a GenerateJob is created, which in its Burst Execute() walks every grid cell and makes four passes: AssignGround - picks the ground type from altitude, moisture, and HardLimit . namespace DiceKingdoms.Game ; public enum GroundTile { WATER , WATER_ROCK , GRASS , SAND , INNER_CLIFF , METEORITE , PIER } PlaceInnerCliffs - places inland cliffs using numberMains , numberExtensions , minDistance , minSpacing . PlaceBlobs - plants trees and rocks as clusters ("blobs"), filtered by moistureRange and minDistance . PlaceDots - places point objects (fish) via a probability mask; flowers are distributed along the way by flowerProbability . ScoreTerritory - computes three scores ( buildSpace , naturalResources , cliffs ) and their sum in ScoreData . Generate returns a GenerateOutput — a job handle. The caller can either Complete() it and pull the layers via GetGround / GetNature , or compare several GenerateOutput s via CompareTo (sorted by score) and keep the best. The second stage - mesh. BuildMesh(layer, biome, …) takes the already classified tile layer and builds geometry. Inside MeshJob.Execute() it walks the four diagonals of each cell ( Diagonal ), classifies corners ( CornerKind ), and assembles the PolygonMesh . Height differences between neighboring cells become vertical walls via WallHorizontalStep and WallVerticalStep . The result is MeshOutput : the PolygonMesh itself and the HeightMap . Both stages are fully deterministic: the same seed and Parameters produce the same island. It applies to cells whose ground type is suitable. 7. docs.text: Island Grid IslandGrid holds the tile layers and buildings of one island and is wrapped by Island , which is owned by a Player . Class relationships Player --get_Island--> Island --grid--> IslandGrid \--owner (NetworkedVar<Player>) PlayerSummary --island--> Player's island GameState --Island(Player)--> Island of a given player IslandGrid Member Type Offset Notes size int2 0xF0 Grid dimensions generationParameters IslandGeneration.Parameters 0x1E8 HardLimit.radius is the first field ( +0 ) snapshotIslandSize 0x298 not investigated arraySize 0x2AC not investigated Methods of interest: Awake , Generate , GenerateJob , CanPlaceBuilding , ExportIsland , ImportIsland (private), SaveIslandToClipboard , LoadIslandFromClipboard . RVAs are in the Internals Reference . Island radius ( HardLimit.radius ) The playable land is limited by Parameters.HardLimit.radius , default 22 . Setting it to 24 in a patch on IslandGrid.Awake produced slightly larger real land through the normal generation path (found with a native hook before moving to BepInEx; the same field applies). Do not resize the tile arrays or scale the grid Multiplying size (an earlier "size scale" approach) caused frustum-error log spam, a disappearing mouse cursor and compounding corruption on import. Raising HardLimit.radius is the safe approach. Pushing land toward the edge of the allocated array (roughly radius 24-26) is the danger zone - test incrementally. See also: Island Generation . Clipboard import / export SaveIslandToClipboard and LoadIslandFromClipboard go through GUIUtility.systemCopyBuffer , which was unreliable when called outside OnGUI . A mod should call ExportIsland / ImportIsland directly and do its own clipboard handling, then use the format page to process the string. Developer cheats The in-game dev console (including saveisland / loadisland ) is gated by two methods on Cheats : Method Effect when forced to return true Cheats.get_Available console/cheat commands become available Cheats.CheckAvailable same gate, second path Both need to return true . With BepInEx a Harmony postfix does this (untested example - check exact member names in the interop assemblies): [HarmonyPatch(typeof(Cheats), nameof(Cheats.CheckAvailable))] static class CheckAvailablePatch { static void Postfix ( ref bool __result ) => __result = true ; } [HarmonyPatch(typeof(Cheats), nameof(Cheats.Available), MethodType.Getter)] static class AvailablePatch { static void Postfix ( ref bool __result ) => __result = true ; } The BepInEx guide covers setting up the project . Multiplayer notes (theory, not verified) Island state is an IslandSyncedBehaviour . The working theory is that the host is the only authoritative sync source, so loading an island string onto another player's island on the host would replace it for everyone. This was never observed working live. True host migration (reassigning the MLAPI listen server) is a different problem class and is not achievable by patching memory.

docs.text: Island Save Format An island code is the string the game's dev console copies to the clipboard ( saveisland ) and reads back ( loadisland ). It is a serialized IslandGrid.SyncData - the same structure that is network-synced between players. Status Fully reverse engineered and validated with decode -> encode -> byte-identical round trips on real islands. Pipeline island code (text) -> base64 decode -> raw DEFLATE inflate (NO zlib header, NO gzip header) -> MLAPI packed-int stream (IslandGrid.SyncData) Encoding is the same pipeline in reverse. In JavaScript the browser primitives DecompressionStream('deflate-raw') / CompressionStream('deflate-raw') do exactly this; in C# use DeflateStream (not ZLibStream ). Packed integers Every number in the stream is an MLAPI UInt64Packed varint. Signed values ( int32 ) are zigzag-encoded first : 0, -1, 1, -2, 2 ... -> 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 ... First byte b Total size Value 0x00 - 0xF0 1 byte b 0xF1 - 0xF8 2 bytes (b - 0xF1) * 256 + next + 0xF0 0xF9 3 bytes hi * 256 + lo + 0x8F0 0xFA - 0xFF 1 + (b - 0xF7) bytes the following n = b - 0xF7 bytes, little endian Stream layout All counts and values below are packed ints ( i32 = zigzag, u64 = raw). buildings[] : i32 count, then count x Building remains[] : i32 count, then count x Building (destroyed buildings, same layout) groundTiles : RLE (i32 totalLength, then runs of {i32 runLength, i32 value}) natureTiles : RLE (same layout) innerCliffs[] : i32 count, then count x { i32 c, i32 a, i32 b, i32 x, i32 y, i32 orient, i32 mirror } Building (used by both buildings and remains ): Field Type Meaning type i32 Building type id (see Buildings ) x , y i32 Grid position of the building origin orient i32 Rotation, 0-3 (see Footprint and rotation ) mirror i32 0 / 1 - mirrors X health i32 Current health (max is BuildingType.maxHealth , see BuildingType ) disaster u64 flag, then u64 payload if flag != 0 Nullable disaster state turn i32 Turn counter The tile arrays are row-major, index = y * side + x , with totalLength == side * side . Ground tile values Value Name 0 WATER 1 WATER_ROCK (a ground tile, not a nature tile) 2 GRASS 3 SAND 4 INNER_CLIFF 5 METEORITE 6 PIER Nature tile values Value Name -1 none 0 TREE 1 ROCK 2 SCORCHED_EARTH 3 LAVA 4 FLOWER 5 FISH Reference decoder (C#) using System.IO.Compression ; public sealed class PackedReader { readonly byte [] b ; int p ; public PackedReader ( byte [] data ) { b = data ; } public int Position => p ; byte Byte () => p < b . Length ? b [ p ++ ] : throw new EndOfStreamException (); public ulong U64 () { int first = Byte (); if ( first <= 0xF0 ) return ( ulong ) first ; if ( first < 0xF9 ) return ( ulong )(( first - 0xF1 ) * 256 + Byte () + 0xF0 ); if ( first == 0xF9 ) { int hi = Byte (), lo = Byte (); return ( ulong )( hi * 256 + lo + 0x8F0 ); } int n = first - 0xF7 ; ulong v = 0 ; for ( int i = 0 ; i < n ; i ++ ) v |= ( ulong ) Byte () << ( 8 * i ); return v ; } // zigzag: even -> x/2, odd -> -(x+1)/2 public int I32 () { ulong x = U64 (); return ( x & 1 ) == 0 ? ( int )( x >> 1 ) : - ( int )(( x + 1 ) >> 1 ); } } public static byte [] Unpack ( string islandCode ) { byte [] compressed = Convert . FromBase64String ( islandCode . Trim ()); using var input = new MemoryStream ( compressed ); using var deflate = new DeflateStream ( input , CompressionMode . Decompress ); // raw DEFLATE using var output = new MemoryStream (); deflate . CopyTo ( output ); return output . ToArray (); } Reading the whole structure (works the same inside a BepInEx plugin): List < Building > ReadBuildings ( PackedReader r ) { int n = r . I32 (); var list = new List < Building > ( n ); for ( int i = 0 ; i < n ; i ++ ) { var b = new Building { Type = r . I32 (), X = r . I32 (), Y = r . I32 (), Orient = r . I32 (), Mirror = r . I32 (), Health = r . I32 () }; if ( r . U64 () != 0 ) b . Disaster = r . U64 (); b . Turn = r . I32 (); list . Add ( b ); } return list ; } int [] ReadRle ( PackedReader r ) { int total = r . I32 (); var values = new List < int > ( total ); while ( values . Count < total ) { int run = r . I32 (), v = r . I32 (); for ( int i = 0 ; i < run ; i ++ ) values . Add ( v ); } return values . ToArray (); } Round-trip rule When editing, always re-encode with the exact same field order. Unknown or unedited lists ( remains , innerCliffs ) must be written back untouched - the game rejects or mis-loads streams that are even one packed int off.

docs.text: Mods Installation Installing BepInEx BepInEx is a mod loader. It allows the game to load mods. You only need to install it once. BepInEx documentation: Installing BepInEx on Il2Cpp Unity Installation steps: Download BepInEx 6.x. Go to the BepInEx releases page . Find the latest release and download the file for Unity IL2CPP . It has name in this format BepInEx-Unity.IL2CPP-OS-x64-6.X.X.zip . Find the game folder. This is the folder where DiceKingdoms.exe is located. Open Steam. Right-click on Dice Kingdoms in your library. Select Manage → Browse local files . A folder will open. This is the game folder. Extract BepInEx into the game folder. Right-click the downloaded BepInEx archive and choose Extract All . Copy everything from inside the archive into the game folder. Make sure the BepInEx folder and files like doorstop_config.ini and winhttp.dll appear next to DiceKingdoms.exe . Run the game once. Start the game normally. The first launch may take longer than usual. This is normal. BepInEx is setting itself up. You can close the game after it reaches the main menu. Check that BepInEx is installed. Open the game folder. You should see a BepInEx folder. Inside it, there should be: LogOutput.txt a config folder with BepInEx.cfg inside. If you see these, BepInEx is installed correctly. Installing Mods After BepInEx is installed, installing mods is usually very simple. Download the mod. Mods are usually shared as .zip or .rar files. Extract the mod archive. Right-click the archive and choose Extract All . Extract it to a temporary folder, like your Desktop. Look inside the extracted folder. The main mod file has a .dll extension. This is the mod itself. A mod can also be a set of files: for example, one .dll plus some folders or other files. All of them belong together. Some mods include a README.txt or similar. Read it first — it may have special instructions. Sometimes the archive already contains a plugins folder. If you see that, the mod is packaged so that you can simply extract the archive contents directly into the game's root folder (the folder with DiceKingdoms.exe ). The plugins folder will merge with BepInEx/plugins , and the mod will be placed correctly automatically. If there is no plugins folder in the archive, install manually: Go to your game folder. Open BepInEx . If there is no plugins folder, create one and name it exactly plugins . Copy all mod files (the .dll and any accompanying files or folders) into BepInEx/plugins . If the mod has its own folder structure, keep it. For example, if the mod has a folder MyMod containing MyMod.dll and an assets folder, copy the whole MyMod folder into BepInEx/plugins . Example: C:\Games\DiceKingdoms\BepInEx\plugins\MyMod.dll Run the game. The mod should load automatically. If the mod has settings, a config file may appear in BepInEx/config after you run the game. You can open it with Notepad and change values.

docs.text: Custom models This page shows how to replace the look of a building with your own model at runtime (tested in game with the Castle). It only changes what the local player sees: footprint, rules and networking stay the original, and other players still see the original model. To give a whole civilization its own models through the game's skin system, see Making a civilization . Getting the original models AssetRipper exports the game's assets (game version 1.0.4 uses Unity 2021.3.36f1 ) as plain files and as a Unity project. Its free glTF export gives rigged units as skeletons only. For rigged and animated models (units, inhabitants, ships, buildings with moving parts): open the exported project in Unity 2021.3.36f1 and export FBX with the FBX Exporter (include model and animation). The FBX SDK crashes now and then inside the export call; exporting in small batches with a restart is reliable. Unit models have the takes idle, walk, run and attack; ships move and extend / retract the plank; the Windmill has its sails. In Blender, import FBX with "Ignore Leaf Bones"; each take becomes an Action. The palette All game models use one material with an 8×8 palette texture ( ColorPalette.png ). A face's colour is the cell its UVs point to; put every vertex of a face inside one cell, near its centre, and use point filtering in Blender. Cell (7, 7) is repainted with the player colour (see Rendering ). Tested observations: (0, 3) renders brown/orange; (0, 4) ("sand") renders clearly yellow in game lighting. Good ground greens: (5, 3) and (5, 4). The in-game light is brighter and warmer than Blender's preview, so check colours in the game. The original roofs and trim use (3, 4); lit windows (5, 0) orange and (5, 1) yellow (the only emissive cells); metal door fittings (3, 6). Blender → Unity axes Calibrated with the Castle's flag: Prefab-local = Blender root-local / 100 , with Unity x = −Blender x, Unity y = Blender y, Unity z = Blender z (in the FBX root space, which is already Y-up). That map is a mirror (determinant −1), so reverse the triangle order when you write the indices, otherwise the faces turned toward the camera are missing in game. In Blender (after importing a game FBX): east = −X, north = −Y, west = +X, south = +Y. The game camera sees orientation 0 from Blender's +X +Y corner, so a gate meant to face the camera at the default orientation goes on +X (like the Viking and Ancient castles). See Rendering . Keep the model inside the building's tiles (a Castle is 4×4: tiles −1..2). What a building looks like at runtime Taking the Castle as the example: Buildings are BuildingVisual objects. The prefab root is Castle <civ> ; pooled copies are named like Castle Viking <49> #0001 , Castle Europe (1) or ...(Clone) . Cut the name at the first < , ( or ( to get the civilization (Europe, Middle East, Viking, Ancient, Maya). The body mesh is castle-<civ>-mesh_LOD0/1/2 (MeshFilters under a LODGroup ), present twice : under Visual and under Damaged Visual . Replace both, or the destroyed state shows the old model. Castle Viking contains two LOD groups ( castle-europe-mesh_LOD* and castle-viking-mesh_LOD* ). Filling both draws the model twice and the copies flicker. Fill only the civilization's own group (fallback castle-europe ) and give the others an empty mesh. The team flag is a separate MeshFilter flag-big with its pivot at the foot of the pole (Europe: local (0.385, 2.38, 0.545)). Move it with localPosition / localRotation onto your model. The King is a SkinnedMeshRenderer under Inhabitant King <civ> . Replacing the mesh Hook: a Harmony postfix on BuildingVisual.Apply runs every time a building is built or refreshed. Replacing the mesh there is enough; doing it again is harmless. Build the Mesh once and reuse it: vertices, UVs (palette cells), triangles, normals. Use IndexFormat.UInt32 above 65 535 vertices and set hideFlags = HideFlags.DontUnloadUnusedAsset so a scene change does not unload it. Mesh.RecalculateNormals() is stripped from this build and throws. Compute the normals yourself (cross product per triangle, summed per vertex, normalized). The bounds update when you set the vertices. Setting MeshFilter.sharedMesh keeps the game's materials (player colour, tints, burnt look). Flicker and missing faces The game camera is far away, so depth precision is low: faces that are coplanar or nearly touching flicker much more than in Blender. In the model: never let two parts share a face exactly (make a footing 1–2 cm wider than the wall on it; do not end two walls in the same plane). At export: push each connected part out along its normals by a tiny amount that is larger for small parts (details on top of big parts), for example 0.0015 × (1 + 4 × (1 − size/4)²) . Missing faces: check the winding (above). Writing every triangle twice (both windings) hides parts whose normals are flipped in Blender. A mesh cleanup that removes "back-to-back face pairs" also deletes deliberately double-sided thin parts; build thin walls as solid wedges or boxes instead. Limits Only the local player sees the model; footprint, flag logic, fire / smoke anchors and the inhabitant's walking area stay those of the original prefab. One mesh for all LOD levels is fine at building size. The destroyed state uses the same model (sunk and tinted); a separate damaged model needs a second mesh.
docs.title: Custom Models

docs.text: This page shows how to replace the look of a building with your own model at runtime (tested in game with the Castle). It only changes what the local player sees: footprint, rules and networking stay the original, and other players still see the original model. To give a whole civilization its own models through the game's skin system, see Making a civilization .
docs.title: Custom models

docs.text: AssetRipper exports the game's assets (game version 1.0.4 uses Unity 2021.3.36f1 ) as plain files and as a Unity project. Its free glTF export gives rigged units as skeletons only. For rigged and animated models (units, inhabitants, ships, buildings with moving parts): open the exported project in Unity 2021.3.36f1 and export FBX with the FBX Exporter (include model and animation). The FBX SDK crashes now and then inside the export call; exporting in small batches with a restart is reliable. Unit models have the takes idle, walk, run and attack; ships move and extend / retract the plank; the Windmill has its sails. In Blender, import FBX with "Ignore Leaf Bones"; each take becomes an Action.
docs.title: Getting the original models

docs.text: All game models use one material with an 8×8 palette texture ( ColorPalette.png ). A face's colour is the cell its UVs point to; put every vertex of a face inside one cell, near its centre, and use point filtering in Blender. Cell (7, 7) is repainted with the player colour (see Rendering ). Tested observations: (0, 3) renders brown/orange; (0, 4) ("sand") renders clearly yellow in game lighting. Good ground greens: (5, 3) and (5, 4). The in-game light is brighter and warmer than Blender's preview, so check colours in the game. The original roofs and trim use (3, 4); lit windows (5, 0) orange and (5, 1) yellow (the only emissive cells); metal door fittings (3, 6).
docs.title: The palette

docs.text: Calibrated with the Castle's flag: Prefab-local = Blender root-local / 100 , with Unity x = −Blender x, Unity y = Blender y, Unity z = Blender z (in the FBX root space, which is already Y-up). That map is a mirror (determinant −1), so reverse the triangle order when you write the indices, otherwise the faces turned toward the camera are missing in game. In Blender (after importing a game FBX): east = −X, north = −Y, west = +X, south = +Y. The game camera sees orientation 0 from Blender's +X +Y corner, so a gate meant to face the camera at the default orientation goes on +X (like the Viking and Ancient castles). See Rendering . Keep the model inside the building's tiles (a Castle is 4×4: tiles −1..2).
docs.title: Blender → Unity axes

docs.text: Taking the Castle as the example: Buildings are BuildingVisual objects. The prefab root is Castle <civ> ; pooled copies are named like Castle Viking <49> #0001 , Castle Europe (1) or ...(Clone) . Cut the name at the first < , ( or ( to get the civilization (Europe, Middle East, Viking, Ancient, Maya). The body mesh is castle-<civ>-mesh_LOD0/1/2 (MeshFilters under a LODGroup ), present twice : under Visual and under Damaged Visual . Replace both, or the destroyed state shows the old model. Castle Viking contains two LOD groups ( castle-europe-mesh_LOD* and castle-viking-mesh_LOD* ). Filling both draws the model twice and the copies flicker. Fill only the civilization's own group (fallback castle-europe ) and give the others an empty mesh. The team flag is a separate MeshFilter flag-big with its pivot at the foot of the pole (Europe: local (0.385, 2.38, 0.545)). Move it with localPosition / localRotation onto your model. The King is a SkinnedMeshRenderer under Inhabitant King <civ> .

docs.text: Hook recipes All recipes were tested in game version 1.0.4 with BepInEx 6 (IL2CPP) in a custom match against AIs, as the host. The page Networking explains which side runs what. [BepInPlugin("author.mymod", "My Mod", "0.1.0")] public class MyPlugin : BasePlugin { public override void Load () => new Harmony ( "author.mymod" ). PatchAll ( typeof ( MyPlugin ). Assembly ); } Private methods are patched by name: [HarmonyPatch(typeof(GameState), "ChangeTurnPhase")] . The interop assemblies make private members public, so private setters can be written. Structs like ResourceAmount can be created and edited directly: var a = new ResourceAmount(); a.hammer = 3; . Read resources island.statistics.Storage returns the decrypted ResourceStorage ( stored , capacity ). Do not read memory directly: the storage is encrypted ( Harvest ). All players: Object.FindObjectOfType<GameState>().Players ; a player's island: player.Island . React to phase changes Postfix the private GameState.ChangeTurnPhase(ITurnPhase) . Phase name: turnPhase.Cast<Il2CppSystem.Object>().GetIl2CppType().Name (HarvestPhase, DisastersPhase, BuildPhase, CombatPhase; WinPhase only when a win is due). For "after the phase was applied", postfix <Phase>.ApplyChanges . The GameState events ( onEnterPhase , onSyncPhase , …) work too. Change harvest income Prefix HarvestData.AddResources : read __instance.TotalYields , write a changed copy back. Gains are still capped by storage. The harvest screen keeps showing the original dice values; to change what the dice show, patch the roll ( HarvestData.Roll / RollResultsRPC ). Give or take resources island.statistics.AddResource(ResourceAmount) / RemoveResource(...) , capped by capacity. Block a player action Prefix with ref bool __result , set __result = false and return false . Example: a prefix on BuildData.BurnBuilding that refuses Castles; nothing happens and no hammer is spent. Find a building by id by walking island.grid.Buildings and matching id.value == (pos.y << 16) | pos.x . Do not call IslandGrid.GetBuilding : it returns a Nullable<Building> , which crashes the game natively through the interop. Type test: b.type.TryCast<BuildingTypeCastle>() != null . Postfixes of other patches still run when your prefix skips the original. To block any build action in one place, prefix the private BuildData.PlanAction . Market trades never call BuyResource ; they happen inside DoAction . Change a combat number Postfix the static ProjectileTypeExtensions.BuildingDamage(Projectile.Type) and change __result for FIREBALL (default 8). The same pattern works for Duration and CombatGrid.MeleeBuildingDamage . Tested: with 100 a single fireball destroyed a Dock (50 HP). The Rules screen's unit page reads the same function, so it shows the changed value. Combat is simulated on every client, so such a mod must be installed on every player's game. Change storage capacity Postfix the private Island.RecomputeStorageCapacities : take statistics.Storage.capacity , change it, call statistics.SetCapacity(cap) . SetCapacity clamps the stored amounts, so never set it lower than you want to keep. It runs after every phase, so the bonus is re-applied each time. Mod the AI without code Put custom-build-orders.txt next to Dice-Kingdoms.exe ; the game reads it instead of its built-in build orders. Format and details: AI . More hook points Camera to an island: cameraMovement.focus = new Il2CppSystem.Nullable<CameraMovement.Focus>(new CameraMovement.Focus(island.grid, 1f, true)) . Night: postfix TurnPhase.Enter and set DayNightCycle.TimeOfDay ( Rendering ). Messages everybody sees: Log.AddMessage(new StructuredText(...)) on the host ( Interface behaviour ). Unlock the console: force Cheats.get_Available to true ( Developer console ). Which mods must every player have Changes to rules that run on the server (harvest, resources, build checks, AI, storage) take effect for everybody when the host has the mod. Changes to combat numbers must be on every client, because each client simulates the fights. Read-only and visual mods (logging, camera, colours, models, effects) are safe on one machine.

docs.text: IL2CPP tips Game classes are exposed through generated interop assemblies. They look like normal C# classes but are wrappers around native objects, which causes a few surprises. Casting as and is work on the wrapper type, not on the native type. A Transform.parent is returned as a Transform wrapper, so transform.parent as RectTransform gives null . Use the interop cast: var rect = transform . parent . TryCast < RectTransform > (); if ( rect != null ) { /* ... */ } Delegates and callbacks A C# delegate cannot be passed to the game directly. Convert it, and keep both objects alive for as long as the game may call it; otherwise the garbage collector frees it and the game crashes later. Action handler = OnClick ; var native = DelegateSupport . ConvertDelegate < UnityEngine . Events . UnityAction > ( handler ); button . onClick . AddListener ( native ); keepAlive . Add ( handler ); keepAlive . Add ( native ); // e.g. a list owned by the same Unity object Your own MonoBehaviours A MonoBehaviour that the game must instantiate (for example to receive Update ) has to be registered first, and needs a constructor taking an IntPtr : ClassInjector . RegisterTypeInIl2Cpp < MyBehaviour > (); // once, in Load() public MyBehaviour ( IntPtr ptr ) : base ( ptr ) { } The BepInEx log prints Registered mono type ... in il2cpp domain for each registered type. Cloning game UI Clone with Object.Instantiate under an inactive parent, strip what you do not want, configure it, then move it to the real parent. The game's Awake and OnEnable run when the clone becomes active, so they see the final setup. Remove the donor's click listeners and tooltip text, otherwise a cloned "Rules" button would still open the Rules screen. Do not clear a button's sprite: BaseButton.Update maps the shown sprite to a state and throws every frame for an unknown one. Font asset and material must be copied together from a live game text; a mismatched pair draws garbage glyphs. A TMP text cut with "..." shows nothing at all if its box is shorter than one line. Size the box from the font's line height. Things that throw or crash in this game string.Format and $"..." with Unity structs ( Vector3 , Bounds , …) throw MissingMethodException: String.Format(String, Il2CppSystem.Object) : the struct is boxed to an Il2CppSystem.Object and bound to an overload that does not exist at runtime. Build log text with plain concatenation and format numbers yourself ( f.ToString("F2", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture) ). Stripped Unity methods throw the same exception. Mesh.RecalculateNormals() is one of them in this build; compute normals yourself. IslandGrid.GetBuilding returns a Nullable<Building> (a struct holding object references) and crashes the game natively through the interop. Walk island.grid.Buildings instead. Runtime Mesh objects: use IndexFormat.UInt32 above 65 535 vertices and HideFlags.DontUnloadUnusedAsset , or a scene change unloads them. A Unity Assert in the game only logs ( Assert.raiseExceptions is false), so a failed assertion does not stop the game's code. Your own MonoBehaviour from a plugin BasePlugin.AddComponent<T>() registers the type and creates it on a hidden object that survives scene changes; an easy way to get Update calls in a plugin. The new Input System is used by the game: read keys with UnityEngine.InputSystem.Keyboard.current.f8Key.wasPressedThisFrame (pick keys the game does not use; F1–F3 are taken). Debugging Read BepInEx/LogOutput.log first; ErrorLog.log usually holds little (launcher and crash-reporter lines). Dump a game object hierarchy once (name, rect, anchors, components) when you need the structure of a screen, and log it with a "log once" helper so it does not spam every frame. Il2CppDumper's dump.cs and Ghidra with the game's GameAssembly.dll loaded give names, fields and method bodies. See Reverse-engineering notes . If the build says succeeded very quickly and nothing changed in the game, the DLL was not recompiled. Run dotnet build -c Release --no-incremental and copy the new DLL (check its timestamp).
docs.title: IL2CPP Tips

docs.text: Making a civilization A civilization in Dice Kingdoms is a number plus data the game looks up by that number. The game only knows five ( EUROPE , MIDDLE_EAST , VIKING , ANCIENT , MAYA ) and throws or freezes for any other number, so a mod has to change a few places in the game code first. This page is the practical guide; Civilizations in the game code explains why each part exists. Everything here is for game version 1.0.4. 1. Pick a number and make the game accept it The civilization travels over the network as one signed byte and 0..4 are taken, so a mod civilization needs a number from 5 to 127 . Choose it from a stable key (for example a hash of authorname.mycivilization ) so it is the same on every machine and in every version of your mod. Then change these places (Harmony prefixes/postfixes; the full list with the exact behaviour is the table in Civilizations in the game code ): Place What to do PlayerSkins constructor, Civilization setter, PlayerSkins.Clone() They derive the biome with a switch over 0..4 and throw for anything else. Build the skins for the built-in civilization yours is based on, then store your number in the PlayerSkins.civilization field. PlayerSkinsSerialization (network reader) Receives the byte and calls the constructor, so it needs the same treatment, or the receiving game freezes. Technologies.TechTree(civilization) Return your tree (or the tree of the civilization yours is based on). It was inlined into Statistics.get_TechTree and Statistics.IsTechnologyLearnable , so patch those two as well. AIPlay.SampleBuildOrder Use the build orders of the civilization yours is based on (AI build orders are compiled into the game). Player.NextCivilization The castle click. A prefix can step through your civilizations after the last unlocked one, then let the game wrap around. Do not replace or patch the player's inventory (see Rules and civilizations ). Rules screen drop-down Append an option and a boxed enum value ( Enum.ToObject ) so the tech tree tab can show your civilization. A sketch of the tech tree patch: [HarmonyPatch(typeof(Technologies), nameof(Technologies.TechTree))] static class TechTreePatch { static bool Prefix ( Civilization civilization , ref TechTree __result ) { if (( int ) civilization < 5 ) return true ; // built-in: let the game answer __result = MyMod . Tree ; // your tree, created once return false ; } } Everybody in the match needs your mod. A player without it cannot read the number. Before a mod civilization is picked, make sure every lobby member has it (for example by publishing your civilizations in the Steam lobby member data and only offering ones everybody has). 2. The tech tree The 22 technologies are shared; a tree picks some of them and arranges them (a slot is a technology, a grid position and links to the technologies it unlocks; a technology is learnable when it has no incoming link or one of the technologies linking to it is learnt). The easiest start is a copy of a built-in tree: take it from Technologies.TechTree(<built-in civilization>) , copy the asset ( Object.Instantiate ) and change the copy. The grid of the built-in trees uses even x values 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (the odd ones are the link ports) and y values 0 to 4. Two slots on the same cell are drawn on top of each other, so move a slot to a free cell. Slots is an array of structs: copy a slot out, change its position , write it back ( tree.Slots[i] = slot ). The game asks for the tree very often (many times a second while the research window is open), so create it once and return the same object. The technologies and their costs are shared by every civilization and cannot differ per tree. 3. Models The game finds the model of everything through the skin registry, keyed by the default prefab and the civilization ( SkinRegistry.GetSkinVariant ; it returns the default when it has no entry). A postfix there can return your prefab for your civilization, and anything you do not replace keeps the look of the civilization yours is based on, so you can replace one building at a time. Results are cached per PlayerSkins object. A prefab is a game object carrying the game's own component ( BuildingVisual , UnitVisual , ...) with its references filled in: the model objects, the materials that take the player colour, sounds, particles, the icons. The game's scripts cannot be added in an ordinary Unity project, so build yours from a copy of the default prefab at runtime: Find the default prefab: Resources.FindObjectsOfTypeAll<BuildingVisual>() and pick it by name ( Civilization models and sprites lists the names), or take BuildingType.visualPrefab for a building. Object.Instantiate it under an inactive parent object that you keep ( DontDestroyOnLoad ), so it stays a template and nothing is drawn. Replace what differs: the meshes and materials of the objects the component's visual and damagedVisual fields point to (a building in two states: whole and damaged), keeping the material setup that takes the player colour ( buildingTints ), the firesHolder positions, the particles and sounds if you do not need different ones. Load your own meshes, textures and sprites from an asset bundle built with the same Unity version as the game ( 2021.3.36f1 ) or from files ( Texture2D.LoadImage , Sprite.Create ). Rules the components follow that a replacement has to keep: a building covers the cells listed in its BuildingType ( localPositions , not your prefab's size); a unit's animator needs the parameters Move, Attack, AttackSpeed and Run (a ship's: Deploy, Sand, Move); a NatureVisualHub is a parent whose NatureVisual children are alternatives the game picks from at random. 4. Icons BuildingVisual.Icon(PlayerColor) and UnitVisual.Icon(PlayerColor) return icons[color.Index] : one sprite per player colour (the array's length is the number of colours the game has, PlayerColors.Colors.Length ). These sprites appear in the build bar, the research window (the "unlock building" technologies show the building from the player's skin) and the unit lists. When you replace a model and want a matching icon, fill the icons array of your prefab copy with one sprite per colour; otherwise the copy keeps the default prefab's icons. The other technologies have one fixed sprite each, the same for every civilization. 5. The name ITextElement.Localized writes the name from the key civilization.<number>.name (a boxed enum without a name prints its number). Add that entry to the string table of the language in use, and again when the language changes (each language's table is created when it loads). Without it the name shows as a missing translation. 6. AI AIs play from build orders embedded in the game (3 per built-in civilization), written for exactly one civilization, so a mod civilization's AI uses those of the civilization it is based on. New build orders would need a game update; there is no hook for adding them. What cannot be changed The biome (ground, trees, rocks, cliffs' base look) comes from the built-in civilization yours is based on; there is no sixth biome. Technology costs and effects, building costs and stats, unit stats : the same for everybody. Only the models (and the tech tree) differ per civilization. Unlocking: the Steam inventory decides which built-in civilizations a player has ( UnlockedCivilizations ). Number of civilizations: 5..127 (see above). docs.title: Making a Civilization

docs.text: A civilization in Dice Kingdoms is a number plus data the game looks up by that number. The game only knows five ( EUROPE , MIDDLE_EAST , VIKING , ANCIENT , MAYA ) and throws or freezes for any other number, so a mod has to change a few places in the game code first. This page is the practical guide; Civilizations in the game code explains why each part exists. Everything here is for game version 1.0.4.
docs.title: Making a civilization

docs.text: The civilization travels over the network as one signed byte and 0..4 are taken, so a mod civilization needs a number from 5 to 127 . Choose it from a stable key (for example a hash of authorname.mycivilization ) so it is the same on every machine and in every version of your mod. Then change these places (Harmony prefixes/postfixes; the full list with the exact behaviour is the table in Civilizations in the game code ): Place What to do PlayerSkins constructor, Civilization setter, PlayerSkins.Clone() They derive the biome with a switch over 0..4 and throw for anything else. Build the skins for the built-in civilization yours is based on, then store your number in the PlayerSkins.civilization field. PlayerSkinsSerialization (network reader) Receives the byte and calls the constructor, so it needs the same treatment, or the receiving game freezes. Technologies.TechTree(civilization) Return your tree (or the tree of the civilization yours is based on). It was inlined into Statistics.get_TechTree and Statistics.IsTechnologyLearnable , so patch those two as well. AIPlay.SampleBuildOrder Use the build orders of the civilization yours is based on (AI build orders are compiled into the game). Player.NextCivilization The castle click. A prefix can step through your civilizations after the last unlocked one, then let the game wrap around. Do not replace or patch the player's inventory (see Rules and civilizations ). Rules screen drop-down Append an option and a boxed enum value ( Enum.ToObject ) so the tech tree tab can show your civilization. A sketch of the tech tree patch: [HarmonyPatch(typeof(Technologies), nameof(Technologies.TechTree))] static class TechTreePatch { static bool Prefix ( Civilization civilization , ref TechTree __result ) { if (( int ) civilization < 5 ) return true ; // built-in: let the game answer __result = MyMod . Tree ; // your tree, created once return false ; } } Everybody in the match needs your mod. A player without it cannot read the number. Before a mod civilization is picked, make sure every lobby member has it (for example by publishing your civilizations in the Steam lobby member data and only offering ones everybody has).
docs.title: 1. Pick a number and make the game accept it

docs.text: The 22 technologies are shared; a tree picks some of them and arranges them (a slot is a technology, a grid position and links to the technologies it unlocks; a technology is learnable when it has no incoming link or one of the technologies linking to it is learnt). The easiest start is a copy of a built-in tree: take it from Technologies.TechTree(<built-in civilization>) , copy the asset ( Object.Instantiate ) and change the copy. The grid of the built-in trees uses even x values 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (the odd ones are the link ports) and y values 0 to 4. Two slots on the same cell are drawn on top of each other, so move a slot to a free cell. Slots is an array of structs: copy a slot out, change its position , write it back ( tree.Slots[i] = slot ). The game asks for the tree very often (many times a second while the research window is open), so create it once and return the same object. The technologies and their costs are shared by every civilization and cannot differ per tree.
docs.title: 2. The tech tree

docs.text: The game finds the model of everything through the skin registry, keyed by the default prefab and the civilization ( SkinRegistry.GetSkinVariant ; it returns the default when it has no entry). A postfix there can return your prefab for your civilization, and anything you do not replace keeps the look of the civilization yours is based on, so you can replace one building at a time. Results are cached per PlayerSkins object. A prefab is a game object carrying the game's own component ( BuildingVisual , UnitVisual , ...) with its references filled in: the model objects, the materials that take the player colour, sounds, particles, the icons. The game's scripts cannot be added in an ordinary Unity project, so build yours from a copy of the default prefab at runtime: Find the default prefab: Resources.FindObjectsOfTypeAll<BuildingVisual>() and pick it by name ( Civilization models and sprites lists the names), or take BuildingType.visualPrefab for a building. Object.Instantiate it under an inactive parent object that you keep ( DontDestroyOnLoad ), so it stays a template and nothing is drawn. Replace what differs: the meshes and materials of the objects the component's visual and damagedVisual fields point to (a building in two states: whole and damaged), keeping the material setup that takes the player colour ( buildingTints ), the firesHolder positions, the particles and sounds if you do not need different ones. Load your own meshes, textures and sprites from an asset bundle built with the same Unity version as the game ( 2021.3.36f1 ) or from files ( Texture2D.LoadImage , Sprite.Create ). Rules the components follow that a replacement has to keep: a building covers the cells listed in its BuildingType ( localPositions , not your prefab's size); a unit's animator needs the parameters Move, Attack, AttackSpeed and Run (a ship's: Deploy, Sand, Move); a NatureVisualHub is a parent whose NatureVisual children are alternatives the game picks from at random.
docs.title: 3. Models

docs.text: BuildingVisual.Icon(PlayerColor) and UnitVisual.Icon(PlayerColor) return icons[color.Index] : one sprite per player colour (the array's length is the number of colours the game has, PlayerColors.Colors.Length ). These sprites appear in the build bar, the research window (the "unlock building" technologies show the building from the player's skin) and the unit lists. When you replace a model and want a matching icon, fill the icons array of your prefab copy with one sprite per colour; otherwise the copy keeps the default prefab's icons. The other technologies have one fixed sprite each, the same for every civilization.
docs.title: 4. Icons

docs.text: ITextElement.Localized writes the name from the key civilization.<number>.name (a boxed enum without a name prints its number). Add that entry to the string table of the language in use, and again when the language changes (each language's table is created when it loads). Without it the name shows as a missing translation.
docs.title: 5. The name

docs.text: AIs play from build orders embedded in the game (3 per built-in civilization), written for exactly one civilization, so a mod civilization's AI uses those of the civilization it is based on. New build orders would need a game update; there is no hook for adding them.
docs.title: 6. AI

docs.text: The biome (ground, trees, rocks, cliffs' base look) comes from the built-in civilization yours is based on; there is no sixth biome. Technology costs and effects, building costs and stats, unit stats : the same for everybody. Only the models (and the tech tree) differ per civilization. Unlocking: the Steam inventory decides which built-in civilizations a player has ( UnlockedCivilizations ). Number of civilizations: 5..127 (see above).

docs.text: Installing BepInEx DiceKingdoms uses the IL2CPP backend. This means you need BepInEx 6.x for modding. BepInEx documentation: Installing BepInEx on Il2Cpp Unity Installation steps: Download BepInEx 6.x for IL2CPP. You can find the latest builds on the github release page . Extract the archive into the game's root folder. This is the folder containing DiceKingdoms.exe. Simply copy the entire contents of the BepInEx archive there. Run the game once. This is required to generate configuration files and perform initial setup. The first launch may take longer than usual while BepInEx analyzes the game. Verify the installation. After launching, you should see LogOutput.txt and a config folder with BepInEx.cfg inside the BepInEx folder. If there are no critical errors in the log and the plugins folder has been created, the installation was successful. Creating a project BepInEx documentation: Creating a new plugin project BepInEx provides project templates for convenient development. Install the .NET SDK. You will need .NET 6.0 SDK or newer. Download it from the official Microsoft website . Install the BepInEx templates. Open a terminal and run the following command to install the templates for BepInEx 6: dotnet new install BepInEx.Templates::2.0.0-be.4 --nuget-source https://nuget.bepinex.dev/v3/index.json Navigate to the folder where you want to keep your project and run the command that creates an IL2CPP plugin structure: dotnet new bep6plugin_unity_il2cpp -n PluginName This will create a PluginName folder containing Plugin.cs and PluginName.csproj . Setting up access to game code (Interop) For your mod to access DiceKingdoms classes and methods, the project needs access to the Interop assemblies. BepInEx generates these on the first game launch, and they contain managed wrappers for the game's native code. The most convenient way is to create a symbolic link to the interop folder in the game root. This lets the project see up-to-date assemblies without copying them manually. Linux ln -s "/path/to/game/BepInEx/interop" "/path/to/your/project/PluginName/interop" Windows mklink / D "C:\path\to\your\project\PluginName\interop" "C:\path\to\game\BepInEx\interop" Now you need to tell the project where to find the game DLLs. Open PluginName.csproj and add following element: <ItemGroup> <Reference Include= "interop/*.dll" /> </ItemGroup> Building and installing the mod Build the project. In the terminal, from the project folder, run: dotnet build Copy the mod into the game. After a successful build, your mod's DLL will be located at bin/Debug/net6.0/PluginName.dll . Copy it to the BepInEx/plugins folder in the game directory. It is recommended to create script for copying mod Linux cp -f "bin/Debug/net6.0/PluginName.dll" "/path/to/game/BepInEx/plugins/" Windows copy / Y "bin\Debug\net6.0\PluginName.dll" "C:\path\to\game\BepInEx\plugins\" After these steps, you can launch the game and BepInEx will load your mod.
docs.title: Project Setup

docs.text: Publishing a mod GitHub release A mod is one DLL plus optional files. Do not commit the build output ( bin/ , obj/ ) or the interop/ folder: the interop assemblies are generated from your own copy of the game and contain the game's code, so they cannot be shared. For the same reason a CI service (GitHub Actions) cannot build a mod that references them; build on your machine. dotnet build -c Release --no-incremental (a plain dotnet build may skip compiling when it thinks the DLL is up to date; --no-incremental always compiles). Zip YourMod.dll (and any files it needs) as YourMod-1.0.0.zip . On GitHub create a release with the tag v1.0.0 and attach the zip. Players copy the DLL to BepInEx/plugins . Thunderstore A Thunderstore package is a zip with these files at its root: File Content manifest.json name , version_number , website_url , description , dependencies README.md The page shown on Thunderstore icon.png 256x256 picture YourMod.dll The mod. Put it in a plugins folder if you want the archive to merge into the game folder by hand. List other mods in dependencies (for example a library mod yours needs) in the form Author-Name-1.0.0 , instead of copying their DLLs. Mod managers install dependencies automatically. In code add [BepInDependency("plugin.guid")] so that the dependency loads first. Tip Test the package by installing it with a mod manager into a clean game folder before you upload it.

docs.text: Internals Reference Classes, methods and field offsets found by reverse engineering the game. In BepInEx code, use the names ; the numbers are for locating the same member in a dump or decompiler. How these were obtained Names, field offsets and RVAs come from the dump.cs produced by Il2CppDumper (input: GameAssembly.dll and global-metadata.dat ). Behavior notes (what a method really checks, call order, data layouts) come from decompiling the same binary in Ghidra after applying Il2CppDumper's Ghidra script. For a PE file Ghidra's address is 0x180000000 + RVA. Anything marked as tested was also confirmed by a live run in game. Build specific All RVAs and offsets are from one game build . They move after a game update; re-run Il2CppDumper to get new ones, and rely on the names. These are from game version 1.0.4 . RVAs are relative to the base of GameAssembly.dll . Methods Class Method RVA Notes Cheats get_Available 0x52A840 force true to enable dev console Cheats CheckAvailable 0x528D40 force true IslandGrid Awake 0x6130C0 good place to set HardLimit.radius IslandGrid CanPlaceBuilding 0x6143A0 IslandGrid ImportIsland 0x616340 private, patchable IslandGrid ExportIsland 0x614900 IslandGrid Generate 0x614EB0 IslandGrid GenerateJob 0x614D90 IslandGrid SaveIslandToClipboard 0x61A690 unreliable (see below) IslandGrid LoadIslandFromClipboard 0x616810 unreliable (see below) Island get_Owner 0x61F7D0 Player get_UserName 0x473BB0 Player get_StartGameReady 0x571AB0 Player get_Island 0x508770 PlayerSummary Update 0x5AA420 PlayerSummary OnSyncPhase 0x5AA1A0 GameState Island(Player) 0x5F2F60 GameState Update 0x5F70E0 per-frame patch point BuildData CanBuildType 0x628760 IsBuildable -> Unlocked -> SteamDemo -> HasResource BuildData CanRemoveNature 0x6288B0 inline check: TREE / ROCK / SCORCHED_EARTH / LAVA BuildData CleanTile 0x628AB0 NatureTile Cleanable 0x61FE70 not called by CanRemoveNature CleanTileTool Use 0x589B90 only fires a UnityEvent CleanTileTool Yield 0x589CF0 BuildingType get_DisplayName 0x5F0E10 BuildingTypes get_Types 0x5717B0 ids in save-file order; did not fire in testing, see below RulesBuilding OnEnable 0x5471E0 holds BuildingTypes at +0x18 GridTransform Transform 0x6105D0 point + rotation + translation Fields Class Field Offset IslandGrid size ( int2 ) 0xF0 IslandGrid generationParameters 0x1E8 ( HardLimit.radius at +0 ) IslandGrid snapshotIslandSize 0x298 IslandGrid arraySize 0x2AC Island grid 0x98 Island owner ( NetworkedVar<Player> ) 0x90 Player UserName ( string ) 0x110 PlayerSummary island 0xD0 PlayerSummary attackers ( List<Image> ) 0xE8 ( _size at +0x18 ) PlayerSummary gameState 0xC8 BuildingType localPositions ( int2[] ) 0x18 BuildingType localPositionsInWater 0x20 BuildingType id 0x10 BuildingType tier / health (maximum) 0x78 / 0x80 BuildingType cost block 0x58 - 0x74 BuildData island grid chain +0xA0 -> grid +0x98 UnlockBuildingTechnology BuildingTypes* / id 0x38 / 0x40 Known quirks BuildingTypes.get_Types did not fire when patched late, even with buildings on screen: the BuildingTypes object is created before a late patch is applied ( RulesBuilding.OnEnable ). BuildData.Unlocked(BuildingType) is called repeatedly, so a patch on it can capture a BuildingType , and from there the BuildingType[] that contains it. Patching early (plugin Load ) may avoid the problem - untested. SaveIslandToClipboard / LoadIslandFromClipboard rely on GUIUtility.systemCopyBuffer and were unreliable when called outside OnGUI . Prefer calling ExportIsland / ImportIsland and handling the clipboard yourself.
